messages.subject_clean: two observers, one of them measured in whole numbers
messages.body_plain:
dear mailing list!
i've encountered the following problem:
in order to prepare a publication on animal densities, a two observer
survey had been conducted in 2009. we were now trying to pool the
observations BUT... one of the observers measured distance in integers,
therefore I assume this dataset to be somewhat rounded. is there a way
to cope with that? i was thinking of adding generated random numbers to
each sample, constructed in a way that they will not alter median, mean,
sd, and variance of the samples, though I am quite sure this would not
be appropriate.
thanks in advance!

--

messages.body_plain:
Sacha:

The heaping you describe may or may not be an issue:  if the truncation
distance is 1000m and distances are measured in metres, then heaping is
not worth concern.  It would be of concern if the truncation distance is 5m.

You can employ appropriate cut-points for both observer's data (Buckland
et al. 2001:109) that reduce the influence of heaping by placing the
cut-points such that the 'correct' distance falls within the proper bin.

The remedy you suggest is a bit like 'smearing' (described in Buckland
et al (2001:269-271)) and available in Distance, but as you suggest it
is an ad hoc approach.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sacha,
(adding to Eric's comment)

Thanks for the feedback (off list), where you mention that distances are=20
up to 20 meters, with esw between 15 and 20. So you are in between the=20
numbers Eric mentioned. Still...

I would really not implement your adding error suggestion. You know what=20
error you add, but you don't know what error you end up, because the=20
observations you add error to already have unknown error. So you're not=20
really getting any closer to truth, you just have numbers that to some=20
extent look less suspicious to a human eye. In practice, for the=20
fitting, things won't change much, and yet you have another convoluted=20
and not easy to justify process to explain in your methods section.

I would rather use truncation points which were something like=20
0,1.5,2.5,3.5,... presumably if the error is just in rounding to=20
integers, that means you end up with the observations in the right bin.

But to some extent I wonder if it will make much difference. Fitting is=20
often quite insensitive to moderate heaping, and you don't seem to have=20
an extreme version of heaping any way. With distances up to 20 meters,=20
if you had rounding to multiples of 5, you'd be in real trouble though.

It is very often that you don't get integer resolution, because=20
distances were "guesstimated", or that you do have higher resolution=20
than that, but it is meaningless. E.g. x's obtained by r sin theta, i.e.=20
perpendicular distances from radial distances and angles, seems to have=20
a precision that neither the original angles nor distances had, because=20
of the trigonometry function involved.

Cheers,

T.

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Quick question. I am interested in applying a binomial distance model wit=
h a normal key detection function to a large dataset of bird point count =
surveys where observers have tallied counts into two intervals: 0-50 m an=
d >51 m. However for the latter interval, half of the data were collected=
 to an unlimited distance and the other half to 150 m.  I'm curious as to=
 whether it is valid to applied the binomial model to truncated data.  Bu=
ckland (1987:382) seems to indicate that the binomial model cannot be app=
lied to truncated data but I am curious whether ideas on this matter have=
 changed in the intervening years.  Thanks in advance for your help.

Sincerely,

Steve Matsuoka

Lit. Cited
Buckland. 1987. On the variable circular plot method of estimating animal=
 density. Biometrics 43:363-384.

messages.body_plain:
Steve, no reason at all why you shoudn't fit a binomial model to
truncated data - you can do that in Distance.  However, the binomial
models in my 1987 paper are for untruncated data, and the analytic
estimators given there shouldn't be used for truncated data.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: Consult about model fit and % CV
messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance-Sampling list,

I am new to Distance and I am analyzing point-transect data for multiple
bird species. I calculated overall detection function and ran 2 analysis
using a suite of 5 models for each. In the first analysis the best model was
the hazard-rate / cosine, and it gave good fit (I can see a slight shoulder)
but the %CV are high (29 -32%). For the second analysis, the Uniform /
Cosine was the best model, and the %CV dropped substantially (10-16%). I
looked at the results and both produced similar density estimates.

I would like to ask in these 2 scenarios, if you would recommend to keep the
models with lower %CV and not very good fit, or the other with better fit
but high CV%. I apologize if this seems too obvious.

Thanks,

Carolina

messages.subject: Re: Consult about model fit and % CV
messages.subject_clean: Consult about model fit and % CV
messages.body_plain:
Carolina:

There is a considerable amount of discussion about model selection on
various list-servers including this one.  Those discussions involve a
variety of metrics, many involving information-theoretic measures.
Recognise the information-theoretic measures assess relative fit (i.e.,
comparing models within a set).  Those metrics should be used in
conjunction with an absolute measure of fit (such as the goodness of fit
tests found in Distance) to get a complete picture of the model most
appropriate for your data.

In your second paragraph you describe a nice example of the
bias-precision tradeoff.  In your first situation you have high
precision (low CV) and high bias (poor fit); whereas in your second
situation you have lower precision (high CV) and smaller bias (better fit).

The hazard rate key function uses more parameters to fit the detection
function and as a consequence is capable of fitting a greater universe
of data shapes.  The cost of having this additional flexibility is
spreading your precious data across a greater number of parameters, and
hence estimating those parameters with poorer precision.

I would rather have a result that on average is correct (low bias) but
with lower precision that acknowledges I am not as smart as I wish I was
(imprecise).  I stand a better chance of my confidence intervals
including the true population size in this case.

messages.subject: breeding pairs and distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Dear listmembers,

I have a methodological question about point counts, breeding pairs and d=
istance sampling.=20
In The Netherlands our main method of monitoring birds is territory mappi=
ng. However, we are now developing a point count method for better covera=
ge (so far only for the agricultural areas, but it will probably be exten=
ded to include all habitats).=20
With territory mapping one counts breeding pairs, not individual birds. W=
e would like to do the same with point counts, as it is difficult to 'tra=
nsform' individuals into breeding pairs afterwards. This means that a sin=
ging male is considered to be part of a breeding pair, of which the femal=
e is not visible, and thus will count as a breeding unit, in the same way=
 as an obvious pair would. We ask people to map all 'breeding units' with=
 a simplified breeding code within 300m from a specified point (non-breed=
ing individuals are also mapped, but will be excluded from the analysis).=
 Points are visited 4 times during the breeding season and species specif=
ic date-limits are set, so that only counts within the date limits (=3Dop=
timal breeding period) are used in the analyses.=20
In the literature I only find point counts counting individuals, not bree=
ding pairs, and nothing about date-limits.=20

I was wondering whether using breeding units instead of individuals will =
pose problems in analyses with Distance?
If so, can they be overcome (for instance by including breeding code as a=
 covariate)?

Thank you,

Best regards,

Maja Roodbergen

messages.subject: Re: breeding pairs and distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Maja, for songbird surveys of this type, we recommend that individuals
are recorded, but restrict this to singing males.  See e.g.
Buckland, S.T. 2006.Point transect surveys for songbirds:robust
methodologies./The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.

Hopefully for most species, estimates of numbers or densities of singing
males will equate fairly closely with numbers or densities of breeding
pairs.  As you note, females tend to be less detectable, and detection
at the point may not be certain, so that singing males satisfy the
assumptions of point transect sampling better than females do.

Steve Buckland

On 15/12/2010 16:44, Maja Roodbergen wrote:

We would like to do the same with point counts, as it is difficult to 'transform' individuals into breeding pairs afterwards. This means that a singing male is considered to be part of a breeding pair, of which the female is not visible, and thus will count as a breeding unit, in the same way as an obvious pair would. Points are visited 4 times during the breeding season and species specific date-limits are set, so that only counts within the date limits (=optimal breeding period) are used in the analyses.

messages.body_plain:
Hello List,

I was doing some search in the list serv, and found some information related
to my question; I have already post-stratified by treatment. However, I am
not quite sure if the setting I have is interfering with the density
estimates.

I am working with multiple bird species sampled at 20 point-transects with
unlimited distance, and the points were randomly selected using a grid
sampling approach.; 9 of these are in a treated area, and 11 in a reference
area. All the points but #. 20, have the same survey effort. The way I have
arranged the data in Distance is below:

*Two regions*: Treatment and Reference; I added a new field under region to
break each the *treatment* and the *reference *in 3 zones (Upper, Middle,
Low; this is RU (Reference Upper), RM, RL and so on for T) and I've assigned
area (ha) to each of the latter.

*Point count*, each has its label and survey effort

*Observation*: I have the label, radial distance, and a field for species.

In CDS I calculated the DF at the global level, and the density, the cluster
size, and the encounter rate post-stratifying by treatment, and then per
treatment per point (sample) to obtain individual density per point, but I
saw weird values (N<D) and would like to ask for some advice. I am also
getting some errors for the encounter rate.

I also ran the MCDS and calculated the detection function at the global
level. I did calculate density at the global level (mean_ weighted by total
effort per strata); also at the stratum (treatment) and Sample
(point-transect).  It yielded awkward results specially when summarizing
data per point (sample), again N<D, and what seems to me high density
values. I got this error, which in my case might be causing problems:

forrtl: error (74): floating underflow
forrtl: error (74): floating underflow
forrtl: info (300): 24 floating underflow traps

 Any insight would be appreciated. Thanks in advance;

Carolina

messages.subject: Inference from ferry data
messages.body_plain:
I am currently analysing a data set primarily collected on ferry routes.
In some areas, there are multiple routes through a wider area giving
fairly good spatial coverage - so I plan to analyse this using the DSM
engine.=20

=20

However, in other areas, there are data from multiple years on a single
route in a big "sea area". The idea is to generate density estimates
along the route for comparisons between years.  I have my project set up
with year as the stratum. As the number of samplers is restricted
(transect sampled on the outward and return in any one trip), I want to
restrict my inferences only to the surveyed area. I've referred to the
Distance help and see that the main effect of this type of set up is on
the variance of the density estimate and that you should remove the
component of variance due to the variability in encounter rate between
samplers by setting the over-dispersion parameter to zero.=20

=20

I'm not confident I've got this set up right. Within a year (stratum),
there are multiple trips - line transects  (2 line transects per trip ,
albeit more or less  the same, on the outward and return) - there is a
lot of variability in the encounter rate between trips. How is this
represented in the approach above?=20

=20

Sorry if this is a stupid question!=20

=20

Many thanks

Kelly=20

--

messages.subject: Re: Inference from ferry data
messages.body_plain:
Kelly:

Not a stupid question.  Your suggestion for the 'other areas' where
there is just a single route (transect) within an area is to do
design-based (CDS) density estimation.

If you wish to restrict your inference only to the region covered by the
effort exerted in that single transect then under these circumstances
(and these circumstances alone, for other readers of the list hoping to
justify the use of single transect survey designs) you would enter the
transits of the ferry route separately.

This is not the type of survey design to try at home, and you realise
the weaknesses of this analysis.  If the animals in your population of
interest were to move just slightly so as to be outside the covered
region from one year to the next, you could conclude that there had been
a massive change in the population when instead the change had been only
down to slight spatial re-assortment.  That is why we bang on ad nauseum
on this list about having adequate spatial replication in design-based
surveys.

messages.subject: Re: Inference from ferry data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kelly, list:

Any variance is the answer to a question, "how would my answer change if I
carried out a set of replicate surveys according to specified rules?"
It's the "rules" for generating the replicate surveys that determine how
you estimate the variance, and how you interpret the estimated variance
when you've got it.

In your case, you have an estimate of density, Dhat, restricted to a
single search strip, from a sample of k replicates in time (but no
replicates in space). You want to estimate var(Dhat).  The variance
needs to be understood as the variance over time, instead of the usual
variance over space.  It expresses how your Dhat estimate would change if
you repeatedly carried out replicate surveys, where each replicate survey
consisted of a different k points in time.

It seems to me that the usual theory applies, i.e. you do include the
encounter rate variance to get a within-year estimate of var(Dhat) from
your k trips.  But there are some points to consider:

1. Does every trip cover the same line length?  If so this simplifies
things, because the encounter rate variance reduces to the variance of a
sample mean: you don't have to consider how line length would change in
your "replicate surveys".  Then encounter rate variance is

var(nbar / l) = var(nbar) / l^2,

where l is the line length on a single trip (constant), and nbar is the
sample mean of the number of detections per trip.  So it just means
finding the variance of the sample mean, which is (often) easy.  But leads
to the following question:

2. Do your k trips constitute a random sample over time?  i.e. is any
trip, on any day of the year, exposed to the same spectrum of encounter
possibilities as any other trip?  If so - everything is easy: the usual
Distance encounter rate variance estimates should be fine.  Examples where
this might not be so easy are:

- Seasonality: are the animals present at higher density at some times of
year?  If so, how are the trip times aligned with the seasonal patterns in
density?  The sort of situation where this might cause problems is when
animal density is highest in summer and trips are also more frequent in
summer.  (This would be a problem for your estimate of Dhat as well as
your estimate of var(Dhat).)

- Autocorrelation, where individual animals are more or less likely to be
detected on one trip because of what has happened on previous trips.  In
your case it seems plausible that the outward trip and return trip may be
correlated - either due to animals remaining in the general area over the
duration, or due to learned attraction / repulsion from the boat?

Dealing with either of those scenarios might take a bit more care.
Others may have better suggestions, but it might be worth considering
(outward + return) as a single transect/trip, depending on the behaviour
of your species of interest relative to the trip timings.

Rachel Fewster

--
